entry.idea: Pipefitters have to stand right next to a pipe and hand-tighten or hand-loosen its bolts, which is slow and dangerous, so Nexterity built a robot that does this job from a safe distance.
entry.lesson: Pull the single most dangerous, repetitive motion out of a skilled trade and sell it back as a rentable machine.
entry.name: Nexterity

growth.reason: The company has only just unveiled its first prototype, so there are no usage, revenue or funding numbers yet.

market.reason: Pipeline bolting is a routine, worldwide task across oil, gas and industrial construction, but the buyer is a specialised industrial customer rather than the general public.

tech.reason: Computer-vision guided robotics that can position itself on a pipe joint and torque bolts to a tight tolerance is solid engineering, but a well-funded robotics team could likely match it in a year or two.

entry.twist: The robot can grip and turn four bolts on a pipe joint at once and packs into a Pelican case, so it can be carried to a job site and rented out rather than sold as fixed factory equipment.
entry.who_pays: Oil, gas and industrial construction companies that need pipeline joints opened and closed for maintenance and repair.
entry.why_now: Skilled pipefitters are hard to find and the bolting step is one of the most dangerous parts of the job, so plants are open to a machine that removes the worker from the hazard.
